title: Mary Magdalene
lead: A woman from Magdala on the Sea of Galilee who followed Jesus and supported his work, stood near the cross, and was the first to see him risen. Later tradition turned her into a repentant prostitute, a picture the Gospels themselves do not give.

sections.b: Luke names her among the women who traveled with Jesus and the Twelve and paid their way from their own means; seven demons had gone out of her (Luke 8:1–3). All four Gospels place her at the crucifixion (Matthew 27:56; Mark 15:40; John 19:25) and at the tomb on the first day of the week (Matthew 28:1; Mark 16:1; Luke 24:10; John 20:1). In John she comes alone while it is still dark, runs to tell Peter and the beloved disciple, stays weeping at the tomb, and is the first to see the risen Jesus. He calls her by name, and she answers, "Rabboni!" He then sends her to his brothers, and she announces, "I have seen the Lord" (John 20:11–18). Paul's list of witnesses does not name any women (1 Corinthians 15:5–8).

Hippolytus of Rome (early 200s), in a commentary on the Song of Songs that survives in Georgian, says Christ sent the women at the tomb, whom he names Martha and Mary, as apostles to the apostles; medieval writers gave the title "apostle of the apostles" to Mary Magdalene herself. In a sermon of AD 591 Pope Gregory the Great identified Mary Magdalene with the sinful woman of Luke 7:36–50 and with Mary of Bethany, and the Western church long remembered her as a repentant prostitute. The Eastern churches kept the three women separate and honor her as "equal to the apostles." In 1969 the Catholic calendar separated her feast from the composite figure, and in 2016 her memorial was raised to a feast. Later writings outside the Bible, such as the second-century Gospel of Mary and the third-century Gospel of Philip, give her a special role as a teacher or companion of Jesus. Historians find no reliable evidence that she married him.
